The Pontiff was welcomed by 40,000 people in Paysandú, Uruguay. Leo's sixth apostolic journey comes less than a month after lung adenocarcinoma surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital.

During his sixth apostolic journey, Pope Leo XIV stopped in Paysandú, in Uruguay, where he celebrated Mass in the Parque París Londres in front of more than 40,000 faithful.

Arriving at the exhibition area in the popemobile from the "Brigadier General Aviator Tydeo Larre Borges" International Airport, the Pontiff made his way through the cheering crowd, blessing those present. When he reached the altar, next to an image of Blessed Jacinto Vera, he centred his entire homily on the key concepts of unity and community.

"Peace is possible and we are called to build it," the pontiff said during the liturgical celebration. He then offered the multitude three symbols characteristic of Uruguayan soil to show how to safeguard and spread the Christian faith today.

The first element he evoked was the "General Artigas" bridge, a metaphor for the importance of building strong bonds and engaging in dialogue with others. The second was represented by the local palm trees, which grow together in groves and recall the communal nature of the Church. Finally, there was mate, the famous traditional drink shared at moments of encounter, highlighted as a deep emblem of familiarity and brotherhood. "An element deeply significant to your culture, around which friends or relatives gather to share," Leo XIV said.

At the end of the service, after official thanks from the bishop of Salto, Arturo Eduardo Fajardo Bustamante, the Pope presented a chalice to the local diocese.

Leo XIV's programme in Uruguay

The packed schedule for the day continued with an intense itinerary of institutional and pastoral engagements. After the liturgy in the park, a visit to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary followed for the unveiling of a commemorative plaque and a greeting to the faithful outside the building. The Pontiff then left Paysandú for the capital, Montevideo, where the second part of his busy official agenda continued.

In the late afternoon in the capital, the Pope will meet the social community of Casavalle at the Parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe. This will be followed by an engagement with the academic and education sector at the Catholic University of Uruguay. Both moments will be a central opportunity for direct dialogue with the educational and care institutions of the South American country.

The day will conclude at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium, which the Pope will reach by travelling in the popemobile to allow once again for an encounter with the public. In the sports venue, Leo XIV will preside over a solemn prayer vigil together with thousands of young people and faithful who have travelled from all over the country for the closing event.

On Sunday, the pope is expected in Florida, about 90 kilometres from the capital Montevideo, considered the "cradle" of the nation because it is where the Declaration of Independence took place in 1825. It is also an important religious centre due to the presence of the National Shrine of the Virgen de los Treinta y Tres. In the square in front of it the Pope will celebrate Sunday Mass.

In a post on X, Le Pen, the presidential candidate for the far-right National Rally party, hit out at what she called a "plan to dismantle France".

Hard left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has called on his supporters to gather in Le Bourget, just north of Paris, on Saturday, where he is set to present his party's new manifesto, "L'Avenir en commun" (The Future in Common).

After launching his campaign in June with a rally attended by 26,000 people outside the Basilica of Saint-Denis, he went on to hold a second major rally in Clermont-Ferrand in the Auvergne region.

That event coincided with the start of the high-school students' movement in France and was also marked by a symbolic visit to the Gergovie plateau, where the Gauls famously defeated Julius Caesar's Roman army.

His choice of venue for this latest campaign event also appears calculated.

It was in Le Bourget that François Hollande delivered his now-famous declaration during the 2012 presidential campaign: "My real opponent is the world of finance."

The statement was intended to establish his left-wing credentials before he went on, once elected, to pursue supply-side economic policies - a first for a French Socialist leader.

Nearly fifteen years later, Mélenchon is seeking to position himself as the candidate of a decisive break with the left, at a time when social unrest is spreading across the country.

Firmly in second place in the polls on around 18%, the France Unbowed (LFI) leader has picked up several endorsements in recent days.

On Thursday, most Communist and overseas-territories MPs in the National Assembly formally backed his candidacy, despite French Communist Party leader Fabien Roussel also running. The Greens, meanwhile, are expected to decide in mid-December on a possible alliance with LFI.

Despite this momentum, Mélenchon still trails well behind Marine Le Pen, who is polling at between 35% and 37%.

'Liberty, equality, solidarity'

A few hours before his rally in Le Bourget, Mélenchon unveiled his campaign poster.

It shows his portrait set against a Gergovie landscape, a backdrop that also evokes a rural France where the LFI vote remains weak, along with a reworked republican motto: "liberty, equality, solidarity."

On social media, some internet users are already comparing it with François Mitterrand's 1981 poster, which showed him in front of a Burgundy village dominated by its church, above the slogan "quiet strength."

'L'Avenir en commun'

While previous versions of the programme placed the creation of a Sixth Republic at the top of the agenda, ecological transformation has now become one of France Unbowed's main priorities.

Among its proposals, the party is proposing to replace existing administrative regions with "eco-regions" organised around the management of water resources. It also wants to enshrine stronger environmental protections in the constitution.

France Unbowed is also sticking to its commitment to a gradual phase-out of nuclear power, although the target of reaching 100% renewable energy has been pushed back from 2050 to 2060.

On the economic and social front, Mélenchon is keeping faithful to his long-standing pledges: to raise the minimum wage (SMIC) to €1,700 pcm and eventually lowering the legal retirement age to 60 for people who have paid into the pension system for 40 years.

The programme has been published without a detailed financial breakdown, but party officials stress that it is a "foundation" that will be supplemented by around 50 documents detailing the various measures.

At a press conference in mid-October, Mélenchon and Éric Coquerel, the LFI head of the National Assembly's finance committee, presented their "revised budget" for 2027 in the event of victory.

It contained roughly €100 billion in additional revenue to be generated through tax measures, as well as €80 billion in additional spending.

In foreign policy, the LFI is continuing to focus on the war in Gaza and Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. It is also proposing to suspend the association agreement between Israel and the European Union.

On Ukraine, the document calls for a ceasefire but says little about military support for Kyiv. It also advocates setting up a new European security framework that would include Russia.

A 'plan to dismantle France'

Mélenchon's manifesto has already drawn strong reactions from his opponents.

In a post on X, Le Pen, the far-right National Rally presidential candidate, hit out at what she called a "plan to dismantle France".

"It takes the process of deconstruction initiated by Emmanuel Macron since he came to power to its logical conclusion," she wrote.

Speaking near Marseille on Saturday, former prime minister Édouard Philippe, who is also running in the presidential election, criticised what he dubbed Mélenchon's "communitarian vision" and his "administered economy".

Referring to his two rivals on the far right and the hard left, the centre-right candidate said he saw "many points in common" between Le Pen and Mélenchon, notably their "hatred of European integration" and their desire to "leave NATO."

Protests continue

Mélenchon's rally comes as demonstrations continue across France.

On Thursday, nearly 200 marches took place across the country as protesters demanded an increase in the minimum wage and wages more generally, as well as measures to tackle economic insecurity, protection of public services and more resources for schools and universities.

Organisers estimated the turnout to be around 1.6 million people, while the interior ministry put the figure at 575,000 demonstrators.

Ukraine's defence ministry said in April this year that the KN-23 has been used in previous attacks on Ukraine, adding that the weapon was "extremely difficult for air defence systems to deal with."

After three years as vice president, Pedro Alliana suddenly found himself catapulted to Paraguay's presidency on Friday following the impeachment of ousted leader Santiago Peña.

Alliana, a former national team basketball player who would go on to lead the Colorado Party, takes office amid a political and financial crisis in the South American nation that was sparked by the collapse of Ueno Bank this week, which froze the savings of half of the country’s adult population.

After taking office, the 52-year-old vowed to tackle the situation before his term ends in August 2028.

It comes as Peña has been placed under house arrest in the capital, Asunción, and is awaiting questioning on Saturday over alleged crimes of breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds, prosecutors said.

Who is Pedro Alliana?

Born in February 1974 in Pilar, on the banks of the Paraguay River, Alliana built his political career with the backing of former president Horacio Cartes, one of the most influential figures in the country and the leader of the ruling Colorado Party.

Before going into politics, Alliana pursued a business career and also made a name for himself as a basketball player, representing the Paraguayan national team in 1991.

Politics was present in Alliana's life from an early age, with both of his parents having served as local councillors.

His first venture into politics ended in defeat in 2006, however, when he unsuccessfully sought the mayoralty of his hometown at the age of 32.

But two years later, he managed to get elected as governor of the southern department of Neembucu.

He later served in the Chamber of Deputies from 2013 to 2023, presided over the lower house, and then led the Colorado Party.

In 2021, Alliana expected to run for the Senate, but he would later recall that Cartes told him he would instead become Peña's running mate. Peña previously said that Alliana could become "the best vice president in Paraguay's history."

Alliana has faced criticism over the number of relatives holding posts in public administration, among them his eldest daughter, Montserrat. The father of four is married to congresswoman Fabiana Souto.

Cartes

Alliana did not hide his presidential ambitions. A year after taking up the vice presidency, he publicly acknowledged his desire to one day take the top job.

In 2025, Cartes openly backed his possible candidacy.

"Pedro, you are blessed," he said at a Colorado Party event, where he called for supporters to get behind him as the "next president of the Republic."

However, the relationship between the two eventually broke down. After Cartes withdrew his support, Alliana distanced himself and stated on 26 October that loyalty should not be confused with "blind obedience."

His luck changed again when lawmakers moved to impeach Peña but rejected proceedings against Alliana.

The attacks exposed basic security weaknesses in connected refrigeration systems, but experts warn that similar vulnerabilities could put everything from supermarket equipment to hospital and data centre infrastructure at risk.

Cybersecurity researchers say they detected hackers probing internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe in the days before a wave of cyberattacks and incidents disrupted supermarkets and blood banks, with evidence suggesting it may have been part of a coordinated operation.

Refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries as well as several blood banks in France were attacked on 2 and 3 November.

Hackers exploited weak cybersecurity and vulnerabilities in manufacturer Danfoss’s AK-SM refrigeration system manager to put fridges and freezers on defrost settings, in some cases temperatures were set as high 50 degrees Celsius.

The incidents forced many grocery stores to throw away spoiled produce from their fridges and freezers and have become a very visible example of how easily cyberattacks can disrupt everyday life by targeting infrastructure systems that are often taken for granted.

For cybersecurity firm Lupovis, the signs point to a coordinated operation potentially involving a state actor — one that was preceded by days of probing.

The company says it saw a period of reconnaissance targeting these systems just days before the attacks.

The company observed over 276 attempts coming from 91 different threat actors matching specific components of Danfoss controllers during this 10-day period. Activity peaking on 26 October, before coming to a halt at the end of the month.

“Between the 20th and 30th of October, what we saw was a wave of what we call reconnaissance,” CEO Xavier Bellekens told Euronews Next.

“We see a huge peak suddenly for 10 days where adversaries are trying the default passwords. They are trying a couple of those vulnerabilities.”

Lupovis operates a system of so-called “honeypots”, which replicate its clients’ online systems and technologies. The company equips them with sensors and then deliberately exposes them to hackers, encouraging attacks so it can track how these systems are accessed and exploited.

This intelligence can then be used to identify vulnerabilities without putting the clients' real systems at risk.

It was through this system that Lupovis, whose clients include the Scottish government, Orange, Telefonica and a number of retail companies, detected what it describes as “reconnaissance” on Danfoss systems in the days before November’s attacks.

“You can think of it as like burglars, driving through your neighbourhood and identifying the houses they are going to go and break into,” said Bellekens.

Who was behind the attacks?

Lupovis then traced what it describes as the digital "breadcrumbs" left by the probing and attacks, finding that so-called "bulletproof hosting" was used — web hosting services that are designed to resist takedown requests and law enforcement intervention.

“On the one hand, you have Amazon Web Services, they are the opposite of a bullet-proof hosting. If you do something malicious with one of their servers, that's it, they cancel your account. Bulletproof hosting is the opposite. You do something malicious, It's out of jurisdiction," Bellekens said.

Lupovis then examined the hosting providers themselves.

“We realised that some of those bulletproof hosting had been used by Russian groups in the past,” says Bellekens.

The company is clear that just because servers are located somewhere does not necessarily mean that the people using it share the same nationality, so they cannot say for sure that Russia is behind the attacks.

“However, there's a bit of a pattern here,” says the Lupovis CEO, “So we are looking for someone that has the capability to attack certain countries in particular.”

According to the CEO, Lupovis sensors in South America, Africa, North America and Asia did not record the same activity. It was only picked up by sensors in Europe.

He also believes the ability to coordinate attacks across Europe helps narrow down the list of suspects.

“You [the attacker] have to be able to coordinate this attack because most of it happened within a 24-hour period.”

“All of this makes us point to an adversary that, to us, is not a script kiddie [an unskilled amateur]. They are not a lone wolf. It looks like a well-planned operation. So a state fits the bill.”

“When we pull on the thread it does look like it could well be Russia. So, that is basically where we're at.”

The incidents come amid wider concerns about hybrid threats and suspected Russian-linked activity targeting European countries.

However, the precise identity and motivation of the attackers remain unclear.

George Nott, technology editor at The Grocer, said the attacks appeared to have relied on relatively basic security weaknesses rather than highly advanced hacking techniques.

"Attackers managed to access refrigeration systems by simply finding their log-in pages on the open internet, and exploiting already patched vulnerabilities and weak passwords rather than some highly advanced technology," he told Euronews Next.

Nott also cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about who was responsible.

"it's still unclear who was behind the attack or what they hoped to achieve. We'll have to face the fact we may never known. With no ransom demand or claim of responsibility, it could have been anyone from a state-sponsored actor to a gang of teenagers 'doing it for the lols'."

Cybersecurity agencies in the countries affected this week have differed in how they describe the incidents. Belgium, Luxembourg, Italy, Portugal and Estonia have called them a “cyberattack”, while Sweden and Ireland referred to it as a “cyber incident”.

The European Union’s Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) has also stopped short of explicitly calling the incidents a cyberattack.

How did the hackers access the refrigeration systems?

Hackers were able to access refrigeration systems across Europe because controller boxes connected to the internet were being used to remotely manage refrigeration units, Bellekens said.

Remote control of such devices is common in today’s increasingly digital world. However, the Lupovis CEO says many of the systems could have been better protected had they been placed on virtual private networks (VPNs) rather than exposed directly to the internet.

“[It] would have entirely mitigated the risk because like a VPN is more complex to exploit," he said.

To make matters worse, many of the systems were reportedly accessible using factory-default credentials, such as "Username" Supervisor" and "Password: 12345", suggesting that basic security measures had not been implemented.

Nott said the problem reflets a wider tendency in the retail sector to overlook the security of connected equipment.

“The security of connected equipment across the retail sector can overlooked — the priority given to more obvious targets such as payment systems and customer data," he said.

Once hackers had gained access to the refrigeration control systems they were able to switch them to defrost mode and ramp up the temperatures, spoiling goods stored in fridges and freezers across Europe.

Could other connected infrastructure be next?

The attacks have raised concerns about the security of other internet-connected equipment, from supermarket machinery to the systems that control access, heating and ventilation in buildings.

Nott warned the future attacks may not be confined to refrigeration systems.

"more and more of the systems that keep supermarkets running — heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems; electronic shelf labels; floor cleaning robots — could all present similar vulnerabilities if remote access isn't properly secured and software patched," he said.

But the potential exposure goes well beyond retail.

"The freezer is not special. It is just the most visible example of a much bigger category,” says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security, a global provider of integrated physical security.

“The same kind of small, internet-connected controller that was used to warm up those fridges also runs the doors, the access-control readers, the cameras, the alarms, the lighting and the heating and ventilation in most modern buildings.”

Sokka said the same weaknesses could affect logistics and warehousing, healthcare, manufacturing and data centres, particularly where connected equipment has been introduced without sufficient oversight.

“In an office, a hospital or a data centre, the same kind of compromise might be a door that opens, a camera that goes dark or an alarm that stays silent, and there would be no spoiled stock to tell anyone something was wrong," he said.

The risk is particularly significant for systems where a digital intrusion can have immediate physical consequences, he added.

Why are these systems still vulnerable?

Despite existing European cybersecurity rules, Sokka said organisations often fail to treat connected physical systems as part of their wider security responsibilities.

The EU's NIS2 Directive requires organisations within its scope to manage risks to their network and information systems, including through security measures, asset management and incident handling.

However, Sokka said many organisations still focus their compliance efforts on traditional IT systems, leaving refrigeration and other and building systems to facilities management teams.

"A lot of organisations still scope their NIS2 work around classic IT, the servers, laptops and email, and leave the refrigeration, the access control and the building systems to the facilities team, as maintenance rather than security," he said.

He argued that the problem was not necessarily a lack of regulation, but a failure to apply existing requirements to connected physical infrastructure.

"The regulation is not really the missing piece. The missing piece is the is treating these physical systems as part of the attack surface the regulation is already asking you to protect, and giving someone clear ownership of them."

Could AI make future attacks easier?

Cybersecurity experts also warn that advances in artificial intelligence could make it easier to identify weaknesses in connected devices and potentially accelerate the development of new attacks.

"AI is collapsing the time between finding a vulnerability and turning it into a working attack," said Gianni Cuozzo, founder and CEO of Italian cybersecurity firm Exein.

He warned that manufacturers of connected devices may struggle to patch, test and redeploy at the same speed that vulnerabilities are discovered.

"The systems I would worry about most are connected devices that stay in the field for years and can be controlled remotely: refrigeration, building controls, industrial equipment, healthcare systems, data centres and parts of energy and transport infrastructure."

Cuozzi said organisations should not rely on patching or network protection alone, arguing that connected devices also need to be able to identify and block malicious behaviour themselves.

"Every device needs to be able to defend itself at runtime and pre-emptively block behaviour it was never supposed to perform, whether or not a patch exists and whether or not the vulnerability is already known."

Antimicrobial resistance, responsible for an estimated 35,000 deaths each year in the European Union, is spreading across humans, animals and the environment, prompting calls for a broader approach to tackling one of public health's biggest challenges.

Antibiotics have transformed modern medicine, making once-deadly infections treatable. But as bacteria become increasingly resistant to the drugs designed to kill them, that progress is under threat.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is responsible for an estimated 35,000 deaths each year in the European Union, with its health impact comparable to that of influenza, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS combined.

"Antibiotic resistance is when bugs can't get treated with the medicines anymore that we usually use to treat them," Fiona Walsh, a professor at Maynooth University in Ireland, told Euronews. Her research focuses on resistance across human, animal and environmental health.

For patients infected with multidrug-resistant bacteria, the consequences can be particularly serious. Doctors may have to combine several antibiotics to treat an infection, but in some cases even these combinations fail.

"Unfortunately, some people will die," Walsh said.

And the outlook is worsening. A study published in The Lancet projects that bacterial AMR could directly cause 39 million deaths worldwide between 2025 and 2050.

Antibiotic overuse in humans, use in animals, poor sanitation and environmental pollution can all contribute to the spread of resistance. Bacteria and the genetic material that allows them to resist antibiotics can move between humans, animals and the environment.

This is why researchers are increasingly adopting a so-called One Health approach, recognising that human health cannot be separated from animal and environmental health.

Tackling AMR

"The nice thing is that there are many different ways to kill bacteria and these bugs," Walsh said. "There are also ways to protect ourselves.”

Vaccines can reduce infections and, consequently, the need for antibiotics. The World Health Organization estimates that better vaccine use could reduce global antibiotic consumption by 2.5 billion doses annually.

Staying healthy "is really, really important," Walsh said, as it can reduce the likelihood of developing infections that require antibiotic treatment, particularly among older people and those with weakened immune systems.

"Bacteria will also fight bacteria and if we have our own bacterial system within our body that's really healthy, then they can help fight infection as well," Walsh said.

"We need bacteria in order to live. We need them in our gut. We need it on our skin. We have them in your mouth. They're really important," she added, warning that excessive antibiotic and disinfectant use can disrupt the body's natural defences.

For Walsh, the solution is not simply to develop new antibiotics, although these remain important. Researchers must also look at vaccines, wastewater treatment and ways to improve animal health across the food chain.

During the Cold War, the theory of "mutually assured destruction" prevented the United States and the Soviet Union from engaging in a direct armed confrontation that would have led to nuclear catastrophe.

In the current age, Gawkowski said, such devastation could be unleashed by AI systems that hack a country's critical infrastructure, plunging it into complete paralysis.

Europe risks becoming a dumping ground for hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades but new research has found a ‘hot’ solution

Wind energy has been described as one of the “cheapest and most scalable solutions” to the climate crisis – but its boom is creating growing concern.

Turbines dotted across Europe and its waters are engineered to withstand some of the harshest conditions, from intense UV radiation to strong wind gusts, extreme temperatures and even lightning strikes.

While around 85 to 90 per cent of a wind turbine’s total mass can be recycled, the durability of the blades makes it difficult for the remaining elements to be reprocessed.

Wind turbine blades are clogging up Europe’s landfills

As a result, many turbine blades end up in landfill sites once they are decommissioned, typically after 20 years of service, or are incinerated.

Annual decommissioned blade waste in Europe is projected to increase from 20,000 tonnes in 2025 to 55,000 tonnes by 2030 as older fleets reach their end-of-life.

WindEurope, the European wind industry association, introduced a voluntary industry-wide landfill ban that came into effect last year to tackle this.

The association is urging EU policymakers to enshrine the ban into formal legislation, arguing it would further accelerate the development of sustainable recycling technologies.

Wind turbines undergo flash joule heating

Researchers have recently discovered a new way to give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life – by subjecting them to a “brief burst of intense heat”.

The study, published in the science journal Chem Circularity, found so-called ‘flash joule heating’ can transform blades – often made from silica-containing fiberglass and carbon-rich polymer resin – into silicon carbide and graphene, two valuable materials for manufacturing.

Blades were heated to about 2,000°C in seconds; at such high temperatures, carbon can react with silica to form silicon carbide, a hard, heat-resistant material.

Carbon can also reorganise into graphene under these conditions, a material known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity.

The research team found that adding the broken-down blades to other materials before heating made the new material more useful for creating new rotor blades.

Just 0.3 per cent (by weight) of the recovered materials was able to make resin stiffer and stronger and improve its resistance to deformation by 27 per cent under tension and nine per cent when bent.

“The mixture of silicon carbide and graphene can be incorporated back into resins for new wind turbine blades, improving their mechanical and thermal properties,” says senior author and chemical and environmental engineer Bing Deng of Tsinghua University, China.

“That is more than recycling – it’s upcycling. We’re turning something that has little value into something that’s worth much more.”

With airline alliances and partnerships, frequent flyers can rack up miles in their sleep.

Unless you’re an actual frequent flyer, you probably don’t pay much attention to loyalty programmes.

And why would you? You might assume that if you’re not constantly racking up air miles, it’s not worth your time.

That’s where you’d be wrong, because it takes very little effort to set yourself up in a way that will earn you points in your sleep, all of which puts money back in your pocket the next time you go to book a flight.

Here’s everything you need to know about the main frequent-flyer programmes in Europe.

Back to basics: Why should I join a frequent-flyer programme?

There are two main reasons to join a frequent-flyer programme: Earning miles, which can be used to pay for things, and earning elite status, which gives you benefits like lounge access every time you fly.

Confusingly, the names for miles and tier status points vary from airline to airline.

As an example, passengers flying with Qatar Airways earn both Avios and Qpoints with every flight. Avios can be used to pay for flights or upgrades, while Qpoints help you move between privilege club membership tiers.

The lowest tier on Qatar Airways is burgundy – to reach silver, you need to earn 150 Qpoints within any 12-month period. For gold, it’s 300; for platinum, it’s 600.

As a silver member, benefits include 15kg extra baggage allowance, priority boarding, and lounge access. You also get a 25% tier bonus on eligible flights, which makes it easier to keep the status once you’ve initially earned it.

As you move up the tiers, the benefits improve.

By contrast, the Air France-KLM travel currency is simply called “Miles”, while experience points (XP) help with your status tier.

The lowest tier is explorer; to become a silver member, you need to earn 100 XP in a year; for gold, 180 XP; for ultimate, you need 900 XP.

You earn more miles per flight depending on what tier you are (meaning you can save more money), while some tiers also have free seat selection, lounge access and additional baggage.

Which frequent-flyer programme should I join?

The short answer to this is: You should probably join all of them.

I’m certainly not saying pull up a list of every single airline out there and methodically make your way through them. But every time you fly with a new carrier, you might as well sign up while booking the flight, particularly now many airlines are offering free on-board wifi to members.

The long answer is: You should pick one main airline, then try to fly mostly with them along with other carriers that are part of the same alliance.

This is because you’ll be able to transfer miles earned between different airlines, meaning miles you earned flying around Europe with British Airways could be used to get money off a flight to Tokyo with Japan Airlines, or to Sydney with Qantas. All three carriers are part of the oneworld Alliance.

And why do airline alliances matter?

You could pick your main airline willy-nilly, but the easiest option will be to look at which airports are nearest to you and see if any of them are a home base for a full-service – not budget – carrier.

As an example, Amsterdam Schiphol is the home base for KLM. If you fly from this airport frequently, chances are you are already flying with them naturally as they will serve the most destinations from the Dutch capital.

By signing up to KLM’s Flying Blue frequent-flyer programme – which is also the same programme for Air France and Transavia – you’ll benefit from the SkyTeam airline alliance. This means you’ll be able to transfer points or miles gained from flying between carriers in the group.

In Europe, SkyTeam airlines include Air France, Air Europa, Scandinavian Airlines, TAROM and Virgin Atlantic, but the group also has carriers like Delta Air Lines and Aeroméxico in North America, plus Korean Air, China Airlines and Vietnam Airlines and Saudia in Asia.

If your nearest airport is Frankfurt or Munich, signing up for Lufthansa’s Miles & More scheme gives you access to the Star Alliance.

That alliance includes European carriers like Aegean Airlines, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, TAP Air Portugal and Turkish Airlines, plus United Airlines, Air Canada and Copa Airlines in the Americas; Singapore Airlines, Air China, ANA and EVA Air in Asia; and Air New Zealand in Australasia.

Should your main airport be Madrid, then you’ll want to join the Iberia Club to access the oneworld Alliance.

European airlines signed up to the scheme include British Airways and Finnair; Asian carriers like Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qatar Airways and Malaysia Airlines; plus Qantas in Australasia.

Budget airlines like Ryanair, Wizz Air or easyJet aren’t typically members of airline alliances, nor do they have frequent flyer programmes in the traditional sense.

However, easyJet now offers “easyJet Plus” membership, which is a set annual fee that gives benefits like speedy boarding, a large cabin bag included on board, and free premium seat selection. Wizz Air has a “Discount Club”, which includes discounts on fares and on luggage after paying the annual fee.

How to earn miles – without flying

The amount of miles you earn while flying depends on a number of factors, such as the seat class you flew in, your airline tier status, and either the length of the flight or its cost.

But it certainly isn’t the only way to earn – for many airlines, it’s not even how the majority of people do so. In 2015, American Airlines sold 58% of its miles to third parties, meaning just 42% were handed out through flight purchases.

Different airlines will have different partners, which you’ll be able to find on the relevant carrier’s website, but they typically cover travel-associated spending, like hotels, car rentals and tour operators. They may also cover retail brands.

Members of the Aer Lingus loyalty programme, AerClub, can earn Avios on Uber rides, by shopping at M&S, and ordering through Domino’s – you just need to make sure you’ve registered to collect Avios with the right partner.

Many hotel groups, such as Marriott Bonvoy or Accor, have partnerships with airline brands which mean points you earn during stays can be changed into miles, although the ratios may not necessarily be 1:1.

Throughout the year, hotels or airlines may run special promotions that increase the number of miles you earn for a set period of time.

While you may get an email about it in your inbox, you can also follow specialty blogs that are dedicated to maximising your loyalty points earning. These vary from country to country, but in the UK, there is Head for Points, while in Germany you can try Meilenjunkies.

These websites also go into detail about various co-branded credit or debit cards you can sign up for to earn miles, which I have not touched on at all in this article because I am not qualified to give financial advice.

All I can say is that it’s a big commitment, and that you should fully read all of the terms and conditions before signing up for anything.

Other ways to earn tier status

Another reason airport alliances matter is that some carriers offer status matches.

Essentially, this means that if you have reached the silver or gold tier with one brand, you might be able to get the same with another without having to match the number of flights taken.

Virgin Atlantic offers status matches for all the SkyTeam alliance airlines. For silver status, you need to book one Virgin Atlantic flight in any cabin and share proof of status; for gold, you’ll need to share the same proof but make a premium or upper class booking.

Outside of the alliance, Virgin Atlantic will also match status on British Airways, Iberia and Lufthansa.

How much are my miles worth, and what can I spend them on?

There’s no way to exchange airline miles for cash, so there’s no actual “worth” set in stone.

Points can be used to save money on flights, to pay for an upgrade, or to pay for the flight completely, although airlines will only have a set number of miles-only seats on each plane. You may also be able to use them at the airline partners where you can earn them, which we covered above.

When people talk about how much your airline miles are worth, this is how much money you are saving by using them divided by the number you have – so you may get more bang for your buck depending on what you use them for.

The blogs mentioned above will have various breakdowns for the different airline miles and recommendations for how to spend them, but of course, it’s up to you.

A few years back, I used my miles whenever I could to save money on flights, but nowadays, I prefer to save them up and upgrade to business class when I have enough.

Frequent-flyer programmes: The top tips to know

  • Pick a full-service airline that operates out of an airport near you, and sign up for the loyalty programme.
  • Take a look around your carrier’s website to check its partners – you might be able to earn points while shopping, eating out, or booking a hotel, not just while flying.
  • Find out what airline alliance they are in, and sign up for the loyalty programmes of other carriers you might fly with. Make sure you link your accounts.
  • Use your points to save money on tickets or to upgrade, or use them at other partners.

One of the UAE's most senior energy officials told Euronews diversification has carried the country's energy sector through months of regional crisis, as Europe looks to the Gulf for secure supply.

The UAE will remain a reliable energy supplier to Europe and the world despite the regional crisis, Undersecretary of Energy and Petroleum Affairs Sharif Al Olama told Euronews.

Speaking at ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi, Al Olama said the UAE's oil exports continued throughout the crisis and that the country is using the experience to strengthen its energy infrastructure.

"I'm glad to say that we have proven ourselves during this crisis," he said.

Away from the cameras, conversations among the senior officials gathered at ADIPEC from across the world were dominated by the threat of renewed military strikes in the region amid the ongoing US-Iran war. Many had resigned themselves to their inevitability, while still hoping diplomacy could find a way forward.

Al Olama was candid about the pressure the sector has faced. "This is not a big secret. We are going through a crisis. The first few months were very difficult."

He credited the UAE's long-term decision to spread its energy mix across nuclear, renewables and fossil fuels, with hydrogen and other future fuels in development.

"To diversify the energy sources was the right decision to make and it has helped in terms of making sure that our systems continue to operate and the services were uninterrupted during the entire period of the crisis," Al Olama said.

He credited investment in diversified export routes for keeping oil moving to international customers, with further improvement expected "as time goes by".

"In the case of our oil exports, it has continued during the crisis."

Lessons from the period are now being built into facility design, the capacity under construction and the back-up held across the system. "We have learned a lot from the current crisis when it comes to the design of our facilities, when it comes the capacities that we are building, when it come to the redundancy in the systems itself."

On renewables, Al Olama said the UAE now has around 8.2 gigawatts of solar capacity, with plans to grow to 20 gigawatts and beyond.

"We are getting some of the cheapest kilowatt-hours that renewable energies can produce in the world here in the UAE and we're only expanding on that," he explained.

"So there are massive projects coming on their way over the next few years."

Planning for AI demand

The rapid growth of AI data centres, a recurring theme on the exhibition floor at ADIPEC, presents what he described as a global challenge for energy planners, and one Europe faces as it races to build its own AI capacity.

"The growth you're seeing is no longer even exponential. It's a vertical growth. That's massive," Al Olama said.

The UAE's answer starts with efficiency, he pointed out, citing cases where AI tools have cut power consumption at some data centres by 40%. Planning for expansion, cooling and the use of existing infrastructure follows.

"This is a challenge that we're living through, but we are planning properly for the future," Al Olama said.

Asked whether Europe could learn from the UAE, he framed it as a two-way exchange. "I think, to be honest, it's not about teaching, I think how governments interact. We learn from each other."

He said the UAE is looking at rating data centres for energy efficiency and climate neutrality, and is sharing practice with European governments. "I'm 100% sure there are excellent practices in Europe that we are actually exchanging views on with our counterparts in other governments."

Al Olama's message to Europe and the wider world was one of reliability and partnership, with the UAE committed to its energy transition.

"The UAE has and will remain a very reliable energy supplier," he said. "We believe in partnerships, in successful strategic partnerships that add value both at both ends."

The UAE plans to bring a series of large solar projects online over the next few years as it works towards net zero by 2050, the same deadline the EU has set for its own climate neutrality.

To retire on 70% of their pay, workers on average wages could need to save more than €1,000 extra a month in Switzerland and more than €600 in Germany. Euronews Business compares the estimates for women and men across Europe.

Mandatory pensions are projected to fall short of the OECD’s retirement income target in 22 of the 30 European countries it studied.

In its Pensions Outlook 2026, the OECD estimates how much extra employees on average wages would need to save over a full career to retire on 70% of their gross pay.

Lithuania has the biggest gap as a share of earnings, at 20.7%, while Switzerland has the highest estimated monthly contribution, at more than €1,000 a month for men on average wages.

The OECD calls this the contribution gap. It is the extra share of earnings employees would need to put into a voluntary pension plan, on top of their mandatory contributions, to reach the target.

How much income people need in retirement depends partly on what they expect to spend. “There is no universal retirement income objective. Instead of using target replacement rates, one could use consumption benchmarks, which are target expenditure levels to reach specific lifestyles in retirement,” Stéphanie Payet, a policy analyst at the OECD, told Euronews Business.

The OECD calculates the contribution gaps, which vary from 0.4% in Turkey to 20.7% in Lithuania among male employees with average earnings. The rates are mostly the same for women. But in Poland and Hungary, the gap for women is 8.6 and 2.9 percentage points higher, respectively.

The gap is in double digits in many countries: Ireland (19.4%), Poland (17.3%), Croatia (15.7%), Slovenia (12.5%), Latvia (12.3%), Estonia (12.2%), Switzerland (12.1%), Germany (11.1%), Belgium (10.7%) and Iceland (10%).

“Where gaps are large, this means that people are often under-saved, and so they won’t have enough to have a good standard of living in retirement,” Professor Iain Clacher of the University of Leeds told Euronews Business.

Among other major economies, the gap is 9.1% in the UK and 6.2% in France.

It is smaller in Bulgaria (4.4%), Slovakia (3.9%) and Sweden (2.2%). Turkey has the smallest positive gap, at 0.4%.

In Austria, Denmark, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain, mandatory pensions are expected to meet the OECD’s retirement income target for men on average wages.

How much extra would workers need to save each month?

Euronews Business applied the OECD’s contribution rates to average gross wages in 2025. The same percentage can translate into very different amounts depending on what workers earn.

At 2025 average gross wages, the estimated extra contribution for men ranges from about €5 a month in Turkey to €1,084 in Switzerland.

The figure exceeds €500 a month in Ireland (€974), Iceland (€716), Germany (€617), Belgium (€556) and Norway (€532).

In the UK, a man on the average wage would need to save about €494 a month to reach the OECD benchmark. The figure is €238 in France, €64 in Slovakia, €68 in Bulgaria, €91 in Sweden, €111 in Romania, €129 in Hungary and €360 in Poland.

Even a relatively small monthly contribution can be a burden where wages are lower. Average gross monthly earnings in 2025 ranged from €1,549 in Turkey to €8,957 in Switzerland. They were €5,558 in Germany, €5,445 in the UK, €4,195 in Sweden, €3,830 in France, €2,078 in Poland and €1,772 in Hungary.

At those wage levels, a retirement income equal to 70% of earnings would be about €1,084 a month in Turkey and €6,270 in Switzerland.

Why do contribution gaps differ?

Payet said the differences are directly linked to how much income employees can expect from mandatory pensions. The replacement rate measures pension income as a share of a worker’s earnings before retirement.

“A lower replacement rate from the mandatory pension system means that you will need to contribute more on a voluntary basis to reach the target replacement rate,” she said.

Professor Traute Meyer of the University of Southampton linked Poland’s large pension contribution gap to state pension cuts after the transition from state socialism to a market economy. She linked Ireland’s large gap to the country’s traditionally low mandatory pensions as a liberal welfare state. She pointed to Sweden’s strong public pension mandates, rooted in social democratic governance, as a reason for its smaller gap.

“Low gaps may also mean only formal workers are protected, leaving many outside mandatory coverage (Turkey),” she said.

Purchasing power of money in retirement

Professor Lauri Leppik of Tallinn University said a small contribution gap tells us little about what a mandatory pension can buy in countries such as Turkey.

Clacher added that “The contribution gap alone does not give a clear picture as the other factor that is important is the purchasing power of money in retirement".

Pension income varies widely across Europe. In 2023, EU spending on old-age pensions averaged about €1,440 a month per beneficiary, according to Eurostat.

That figure covers people already receiving a pension, including those with shorter careers. The OECD benchmark is for employees entering the labour market who go on to complete a full career.

Retirement poverty

Meyer pointed to the risk of poverty in retirement.

“Research consistently shows that voluntary retirement saving is insufficient, especially among lower earners. People underestimate future needs, prioritise current demands, distrust private schemes or lack the means to save,” she told Euronews Business.

What could change before workers retire?

The contribution gap is a forward-looking measure. It does not tell us anything about current pensioners. “It is based on expected replacement rates for workers entering the labour force today, assuming the rules of the pension system will remain the same until these workers retire,” Payet said.

The projections include changes already written into law, including scheduled increases in retirement ages. Professor Marek Góra of the Warsaw School of Economics said further changes could affect how much workers need to save. In his view, higher retirement ages would reduce the need for extra savings, while lower replacement rates would increase it.

“As a result, the actual need for voluntary additional retirement savings is less clear-cut than the estimates suggest,” he said.

How does the contribution gap work?

Payet gave the example of an average earner whose mandatory pension is expected to replace 50% of their earnings. Under the assumptions in her example, putting about 9% of earnings into a defined contribution pension plan from age 22 until retirement would cover the remaining 20 percentage points.

Take a worker earning €3,000 a month just before retirement. The 70% target would give them a gross retirement income of €2,100 a month. If their mandatory pension paid €1,500 a month, the shortfall would be €600 a month.

At a wage of €3,000, a 9% contribution comes to €270 a month. The worker would save the same share of earnings throughout their career, so the amount in euros would be lower when they earned less. Under the assumptions in the example, those contributions and their investment returns would provide the extra €600 a month in retirement.
